nodes.name: TiN synthesis
nodes.procedure: The commercial titanium dioxide was annealed in NH₃ atmosphere at 800°C for 1 h with a heating rate of 3°C min⁻¹ in a tube furnace to produce the TiN.
nodes.source_text: 2.1 | Synthesis of TiN The commercial titanium dioxide was annealed in NH3 atmosphere at 800°C for 1 h with a heating rate of 3°C min⁻¹ in a tube furnace to produce the TiN.

nodes.name: N-vacancy creation in TiN
nodes.procedure: The synthesized TiN powder (100 mg) was sealed in Ti foil, loaded onto a quartz boat, and thermally shocked at 1273 K for 30 s with a movable hot bed. Immediately, the sample was rapidly cooled to 77 K by transferring the hot bed into liquid nitrogen, thereby creating N-vacancies. The whole thermal shock process was conducted under a nitrogen atmosphere, and the rapid transition from heating to cooling was completed within seconds. The final product was denoted as TiN - V_N.

nodes.name: Pt loading and HTS on TiN-V_N
nodes.procedure: The prepared TiN-V_N powder (100 mg) was dispersed in 30 mL of deionized water and stirred for 30 min to form a uniform suspension. Subsequently, 125 μL H₂PtCl₆ solution with a concentration of 40 mg mL⁻¹ was added to the suspension. The mixture was magnetically stirred at room temperature overnight, followed by rapid freezing in liquid nitrogen to form the encapsulated ice. The ice was then removed through vacuum freeze-drying. The subsequent synthetic procedure for Pt@TiN - V_N via the nonequilibrium HTS method is identical to that for TiN- V_N (sealed in Ti foil, thermally shocked at 1273 K for 30 s under N₂ atmosphere, then quenched in liquid nitrogen).

nodes.name: Pt@TiN synthesis
nodes.procedure: The as-prepared TiN powder (100 mg) was dispersed in 30 mL of deionized water and stirred for 30 min to form a uniform suspension. Next, 125 μL H₂PtCl₆ solution with a concentration of 40 mg mL⁻¹ was added and magnetically stirred for 1 h. Subsequently, the sodium borohydride powder (0.25 g) was rapidly added to the above solution, followed by magnetic stirring at room temperature for 12 h. The as-obtained samples were washed with ethanol and deionized water through centrifugation and then dried overnight in a vacuum oven at 60°C.

nodes.characterization_summary: XRD pattern of Pt@TiN-V_N shows diffraction peaks of cubic TiN (PDF# 38-1420) and additional peaks at 39.7°, 46.2°, and 67.4° assigned to cubic Pt (PDF# 04-0802).
nodes.evidence_snippet: The X-ray diffraction (XRD) technique was first employed to investigate the crystal structure of the catalysts. The diffraction peaks of TiN-V_N after HTS treatment and pristine TiN (Figure S1) are both well matched with cubic TiN (PDF# 38-1420).

nodes.characterization_summary: SEM image of Pt@TiN-V_N shows morphology (Figure 1C).
nodes.evidence_snippet: As further shown by SEM (Figure 1C) and transmission electron microscopy (TEM) in Figure S5, Pt NPs show better dispersion on TiN-V_N than on TiN without N-vacancies.

nodes.characterization_summary: AC-HAADF-STEM images resolve lattice fringes of TiN(111) at 2.43 Å and Pt(111) at 2.30 Å.
nodes.evidence_snippet: Meanwhile, aberration-corrected high-angle annular dark-field scanning transmission electron microscopy (AC-HAADF-STEM) images in Figures 1D and 1E clearly resolve the lattice fringes of the TiN(111) and Pt(111) planes, exhibiting interplanar spacings of 2.43 and 2.30 Å, respectively.

nodes.characterization_summary: SAED presents diffraction rings assigned to (111) and (200) facets of TiN, and (111) facet of Pt.
nodes.evidence_snippet: The selected area electron diffraction (SAED) in Figure 1F presents diffraction rings that could be assigned to the (111) and (200) facets of TiN, along with (111) facet of Pt.

nodes.characterization_summary: HAADF-STEM shows uniform dispersion of Pt NPs with size 3.7±1.2 nm.
nodes.evidence_snippet: The insert diagram in Figure 1G shows the size of the Pt NPs to be 3.7±1.2 nm.

nodes.characterization_summary: Elemental mapping reveals homogeneous distribution of Ti, N, and Pt.
nodes.evidence_snippet: The corresponding elemental mapping images (Figure 1H) reveal a homogeneous distribution of Ti, N, and Pt.

nodes.characterization_summary: Pt content in Pt@TiN-V_N determined to be 1.44 wt%.
nodes.evidence_snippet: The Pt content in Pt@TiN-V_N was determined to be 1.44 wt% by inductively coupled plasma optical emission spectroscopy (ICP-OES) (Table S1).

nodes.characterization_summary: Pt L3 edge XANES shows absorption edge of Pt@TiN-V_N closely aligns with metallic Pt foil, indicating near-zero valence state.
nodes.evidence_snippet: The Pt L3 edge XANES spectra show that the absorption edge of Pt@TiN-V_N closely aligns with that of metallic Pt foil, suggesting that the Pt NPs predominantly exhibit a near-zero valence state (Figure 2A).

nodes.characterization_summary: Pt L3 edge EXAFS shows peak at 2.66 Å indicative of Pt-Pt coordination.
nodes.evidence_snippet: A distinct peak centered at 2.66 Å emerges in the R-space of the Pt L3 edge extended X-ray absorption fine structure (EXAFS) spectrum for Pt@TiN-V_N, indicative of typical Pt-Pt coordination (Figure 2B and Table S2).

nodes.characterization_summary: Pt@TiN-V_N exhibits pronounced EPR signal at g=2.004 evidencing unpaired electrons at adjacent Ti sites confirming N-vacancies.
nodes.evidence_snippet: In contrast, the Pt@TiN-V_N catalyst exhibits a pronounced EPR signal at g = 2.004, evidencing unpaired electrons at the adjacent Ti sites.

nodes.characterization_summary: N 1s XPS shows lattice nitrogen (Ti-N + Ti-N-O) area ratio 68.96% in Pt@TiN-V_N vs 75.75% in Pt@TiN reflecting N depletion. Ti 2p shows positive shift in Pt@TiN-V_N indicating weaker metal-support interaction. Pt 4f peaks in Pt@TiN-V_N shift negatively by ~0.45 eV vs Pt@TiN (Pt⁰ at 71.16/74.51 eV).
nodes.evidence_snippet: The integral area ratios of lattice nitrogen (Ti-N and Ti-N-O) in Pt@TiN-V_N and Pt@TiN are 68.96% and 75.75%, respectively... For the high-resolution Ti 2p spectrum (Figure 2F), the observed positive shift in Ti 2p binding energies of Pt@TiN-V_N relative of Pt@TiN implies a weaker metal-support interaction... In the fine-scanned Pt 4f spectrum of Pt@TiN (Figure 2G), the peaks located at 71.61 and 74.96 eV can be attributed to the 4f7/2 and 4f5/2 of Pt⁰... all Pt 4f peaks in Pt@TiN-V_N manifest a negative shift of approximately 0.45 eV.

nodes.characterization_summary: In situ Raman under acidic conditions shows O-H stretching (3000-3800 cm⁻¹), Pt-H vibrations (2100-2200 cm⁻¹), and Pt-H₃O⁺ interaction (1500-1600 cm⁻¹) with intensified signals for Pt@TiN-V_N.
nodes.evidence_snippet: In situ Raman spectroscopy under acidic conditions was carried out to probe the interfacial hydration structure and its impact on proton transport.

properties.peaks_observed: Sharp peaks matching Pt and TiN references

nodes.characterization_summary: ECSA of Pt@TiN-V_N is 46.13 m² g_Pt⁻¹ calculated from H_UPD region, higher than 20 wt% Pt/C (36.49 m² g_Pt⁻¹).
nodes.evidence_snippet: the electrochemically active surface area (ECSA), calculated from the hydrogen underpotential deposition (H_UPD) region (Figure S11), of Pt@TiN-V_N (46.13 m² g_Pt⁻¹) is higher than that of 20 wt% Pt/C (36.49 m² g_Pt⁻¹).

nodes.characterization_summary: Charge transfer resistance R_ct of Pt@TiN-V_N is 59.9 Ω, lower than Pt@TiN (71.9 Ω).
nodes.evidence_snippet: The charge transfer resistance (R_ct) of Pt@TiN-V_N (59.9 Ω) was lower than that of Pt@TiN (71.9 Ω), demonstrating that Pt@TiN-V_N possesses enhanced solid-liquid interfacial electron transfer ability.
